8. Here it should also be remembered that the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act came into operation when Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 was in force and governed the agricultural land and that is why homesteads which were within the ambit of section 182 of, the BT Act were kept outside the ambit of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Such a homestead land is not a non-agricultural land as defined in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Thereafter came the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 16. The term home stead is not used in that section as a generic term descriptive of a particular kind of land, but was intended to denote any, land used by the raiyat of under-raiyat for residential purposes, The scheme of that section was to divide homestead lands into two classes, (1) those comprised in the raiyati-holding, and (2) those outside the raiyat holding. Thus a homestead land held by a raiyat otherwise than as a raiyati holding and the homestead land held by a raiyat were governed by that section and those homestead lands were kept outside the definition of Non-Agricultural land as contained in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. At the time of enactment of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the BT Act was in operation and the homestead lands governed by the BT Act were kept outside the ambit of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In 1950 the parliament passed the East Bengal Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and from the date of coming into force of the whole of Part V in any area, the BT Act stands repealed in that area. By 1964 the Part V was enforced throughout country so, BT Act stands repealed entirely in Bangladesh from that period. Even after the repeal of BT Act by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there has been no corresponding change in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act although the provisions of BT Act have been repealed and replaced by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Thus in interpreting section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act today one must read section 2(4)(a) as a homestead to which the provisions of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, (VIII of 1985) would have applied instead of the word 'apply'. Thus, from the scheme and  definition of 'non-agricultural land' as given in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it is crystal clear that homestead land outside the raiyati-holding Situated in the village are not non-agricultural land ie they are agricultural land or land of raiyati holding. So, a transfer of homestead land by a raiyat beyond the Municipality is attracted by section 96 of the Act and not by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land can be claimed only under the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and pre-emption in respect of raiyati holding ie agricultural land can only be claimed under section 96 of the Act. The view taken by me gets support from the decision reported in 30 DLR 75, wherein it has been held that homestead being part of the holding of a raiyat is not excluded from the operation of section 96 of the Act. Similarly, in a recent decision reported in 1 MLR 72, another Single Bench of this Division has held that suit holding being homestead situated in the rural area is an agricultural land and section 96 of the Act is only available. It thus, appears that the correct legal position is that a homestead situated in a village shall be governed by the provisions of section 96 of the Act, be it held by a raiyat as a raiyati-holding or independently of a raiyati holding whereas section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal areas. In the instant case there is no dispute that the case land although a homestead is situated in a village and, as such, is a raiyati land within a village and so section 96 of the Act is attracted.
